title: Development of a larval fathead minnow optomotor response assay for assessing visual function
author: Krzykwa, Jeffries

steps.title: Prepare larval fish stock
steps.instruction: Incubate fathead minnow embryos (<24 h post‑fertilization) in an aerated beaker at 27 °C with a 16 h light : 8 h dark cycle until hatch; transfer hatchlings to crystalizing dishes containing 250 mL dechlorinated municipal water (10 larvae per dish), perform 80 % water changes daily, and feed 1.06 mg Artemia nauplii per larva twice daily starting at 6 days post‑fertilization.

steps.title: Feed fish before assay
steps.instruction: On assay mornings, feed the larvae for 1 hour before starting measurements and limit video recordings to the number that can be captured within 6 hours after the morning feeding.

steps.title: Set up OMR chamber environment
steps.instruction: Place each OMR chamber in a Panasonic MIR‑254 incubator set to 27 °C with the incubator lights turned off; mount the rotating drum (100 mm tall × 88 mm inner diameter) with alternating black/white stripes, motor, and GoPro Hero 5 camera on plywood that has an opening for light entry; position IKEA Nävlinge LED spotlights (warm white, 2700 K) so they emit no heat, and dim the light to approximately 590 lx by placing a sheet of white printer paper beneath the chamber.

steps.title: Assemble recording vessel and lighting
steps.instruction: Use a custom glass vessel (36 mm wide × 75 mm tall) inside the rotating drum; fill the vessel with 10 mL of fresh, warmed, dechlorinated municipal water; attach an identification card to the vessel and record the ID at the start of each video.

steps.title: Record optomotor response
steps.instruction: Transfer an individual larva to the prepared vessel and place it in the recording arena; start video recording with the GoPro; run the drum at 10 rpm for a total of 14 minutes: the first 9 minutes have a constant rotation direction (4 minutes acclimation followed by 5 minutes following‑time measurement), then change the drum rotation direction every minute for the final 5 minutes to measure response latency.

steps.title: Convert videos to TIFF stacks
steps.instruction:
After recording, convert each MP4 file to a 10 fps TIFF stack using ffmpeg via the following batch script (which skips the first 4 minutes to exclude acclimation):

@echo off
setlocal enabledelayedexpansion
for %%f in (*.MP4) do ffmpeg -y -ss 00:04:00 -i "%%f" -r 10 -qscale 0 -vf scale=825:464 "%%~nf_10fps.avi"
for %%f in (*.AVI) do ffmpeg -i "%%f" -pix_fmt rgba -compression_algo deflate "%%~nf_%%05d.tiff"
for %%a in (*.TIFF) do (
  set f=%%a
  set g=!f:~0,8!
  md "!g!" 2>nul
  move "%%a" "!g!"
)
pause

This script also moves each TIFF file into a folder named after the original MP4 for easy tracking.

steps.title: Analyze TIFF stacks in ImageJ
steps.instruction: Import each TIFF stack into ImageJ as a virtual stack; using the stack, record the slice numbers where the fish changes direction and note whether it follows or opposes the stripe direction in an Excel sheet; for latency videos, also record the slice where the stripe direction changes; convert slice counts to seconds by dividing by the 10 fps frame rate.

steps.title: Optional: manual video timing method
steps.instruction: Alternatively, watch the original video at reduced speed and time fish direction changes with a stopwatch; note that this method was found to be stressful for the technician and slower than the TIFF‑stack approach.
